items.followUp: Define cofactor and distinguish between a co-enzyme and a prosthetic group.

rubric.why: A co-enzyme is identified as an organic, non-protein helper of an enzyme.
rubric.description: Defines a co-enzyme as an organic, non-protein substance that assists an enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as an organic non-protein substance associated with enzyme activity.

rubric.why: An appropriate example completes the response.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as NAD, FAD, or co-enzyme A.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: A co-enzyme is a small organic, non-protein substance that associates with an enzyme and helps it carry out a reaction.
Examples include NAD, FAD and co-enzyme A.

items.followUp: What are insoluble dietary fibres? Give two examples.

rubric.why: Solubility in water is the defining feature asked about.
rubric.description: States that soluble dietary fibres dissolve in water, often forming a gel.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they dissolve in water or form a gel in water.

rubric.why: Pectin and gums are examples of soluble dietary fibre.
rubric.description: Gives two suitable examples, such as pectin and gums.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correct examples.

modelAnswer: Soluble dietary fibres are fibres that dissolve in water and may form a gel.
Examples include pectin and gums.

items.followUp: State two ways in which roots are adapted for absorbing water and mineral salts.

rubric.why: This identifies what root hairs are and where they arise.
rubric.description: Defines root hairs as thin extensions or outgrowths of root epidermal cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as extensions of root epidermal cells.

rubric.why: Their absorption role and increased surface area are their key functions.
rubric.description: States that they absorb water and mineral salts and/or increase the root's absorptive surface area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct absorption function or the increased-surface-area function.

modelAnswer: Root hairs are thin extensions of the epidermal cells of a root.
They absorb water and mineral salts from the soil and increase the root's surface area for absorption.

items.followUp: Name two proteins found in blood plasma and state one function of either.

rubric.why: These are three important proteins present in blood plasma.
rubric.description: Names two correct plasma proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two of albumin, globulin and fibrinogen.

rubric.why: A further correct plasma protein name completes the list.
rubric.description: Names a third correct plasma protein.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the remaining protein from albumin, globulin or fibrinogen.

modelAnswer: Important proteins present in blood plasma include albumins, globulins and fibrinogen.

items.followUp: Explain the tissue level and organ-system level of organization, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: An organ consists of tissues working together to perform a function.
rubric.description: Defines an organ as a group of different tissues working together for a specific function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition of an organ.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates the organ level.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of an organ.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an appropriate example, such as stomach, heart, leaf or kidney.

rubric.why: An organ system consists of organs working together to perform related functions.
rubric.description: Defines an organ system as a group of organs working together.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition of an organ system.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates the organ-system level.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of an organ system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an appropriate example.

modelAnswer: An organ is a structure made of different tissues working together to perform a specific function; for example, the stomach.
An organ system is a group of organs working together to perform related functions; for example, the digestive system.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and two functions of mitochondria and chloroplasts.

rubric.why: Centrioles are described as cylindrical cell structures.
rubric.description: Describes the structure or location of centrioles, such as cylindrical bodies near the nucleus, usually in pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct structural or positional feature.

rubric.why: Centrioles organize spindle formation during cell division and can form basal bodies.
rubric.description: States a correct function of centrioles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for spindle organization during cell division or formation of basal bodies for cilia or flagella.

rubric.why: A vacuole is a membrane-bound sac; its membrane is the tonoplast.
rubric.description: Describes vacuoles as membrane-bound sacs and/or names the tonoplast.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct structural feature of a vacuole.

rubric.why: Vacuoles contain cell sap, including water and dissolved substances.
rubric.description: Identifies the contents of a vacuole as cell sap or water with dissolved substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correct contents.

rubric.why: Vacuoles have storage roles and help maintain turgidity in plant cells.
rubric.description: States a storage function or the role of vacuoles in maintaining turgor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct function.

modelAnswer: Centrioles are small cylindrical structures, usually found as a pair near the nucleus in animal cells.
They organize spindle formation during cell division and can form basal bodies for cilia and flagella.
A vacuole is a membrane-bound sac; its membrane is called the tonoplast.
It contains cell sap, which includes water and dissolved substances.
Vacuoles store materials such as water, food and wastes; the large central vacuole in plant cells also helps maintain turgor.

items.followUp: State the main rules for writing the scientific name of an organism, using humans as an example.

rubric.why: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-word scientific name.
rubric.description: Defines binomial nomenclature as a system of naming organisms with two words.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the two-word scientific-name definition.

rubric.why: The first word is the genus name and begins with a capital letter.
rubric.description: States that the genus name comes first and begins with a capital letter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this naming rule.

rubric.why: The second word is the species name and begins with a lowercase letter.
rubric.description: States that the species name comes second and begins with a lowercase letter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this naming rule.

rubric.why: Scientific names are italicized in print or underlined when handwritten.
rubric.description: States the formatting rule for scientific names.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for italicizing printed names or underlining handwritten names.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of giving each organism a two-word scientific name.
The first word is the genus name and begins with a capital letter.
The second word is the species name and begins with a lowercase letter.
The two words are italicized in print; when handwritten, they are underlined separately.

items.followUp: Compare alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation, giving the products of each.

rubric.why: Anaerobic respiration occurs in the absence of oxygen.
rubric.description: Defines anaerobic respiration or fermentation as the breakdown of glucose without oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it occurs without oxygen.

rubric.why: Fermentation incompletely breaks down glucose and releases relatively little energy.
rubric.description: States that glucose is incompletely broken down or that little energy is released.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either key feature.

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation in yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.description: Identifies alcoholic fermentation and its products or organism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming this type with ethanol and carbon dioxide as products, or correctly identifying yeast as its example.

rubric.why: The alcoholic fermentation products are ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.description: Gives the products of alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ethanol and carbon dioxide are produced.

rubric.why: Lactic acid fermentation occurs in muscle cells when oxygen is insufficient and produces lactic acid.
rubric.description: Identifies lactic acid fermentation and its product or occurrence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming this type and stating that it produces lactic acid, commonly in muscles.

modelAnswer: Anaerobic respiration, or fermentation, is the incomplete breakdown of glucose in the absence of oxygen and releases a small amount of energy.
There are two main types: alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.
In yeast, alcoholic fermentation converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide, releasing energy: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy.
In muscle cells when oxygen is insufficient, lactic acid fermentation converts glucose into lactic acid, releasing energy: glucose → lactic acid + energy.
